rows.title: Extremal maximal-matchings conjecture for benzenoid chains
rows.record_statement:
Let $B_n$ be a benzenoid chain of length $n$, and let $H_n$ denote the helicene benzenoid chain of length $n$. For a graph $G$, write $Psi(G)$ for its number of maximal matchings.

**Extremal maximal-matchings conjecture.** For every benzenoid chain $B_n$ of length $n$,

$$
\Psi(H_n) \leq \Psi(B_n).
$$

The conjecture asserts that the helicene has the smallest number of maximal matchings among all benzenoid chains of the same length. The surrounding discussion presents this as an unresolved extremal problem and notes that maximal matchings appear to decrease as the number of kinky hexagons increases, while their value may also depend on the direction of successive turns.
rows.source: Tomislav Došlić and Taylor Short, “Maximal matchings in polyspiro and benzenoid chains”, arXiv:1511.00590 (2015).
rows.what_was_proved: Among benzenoid chains with n hexagons, the helicene has the fewest maximal matchings. Lean proves: for every finite simple graph G carrying a hexagon-chain witness of length n (an ordered list of n six-cycles covering all vertices and edges, consecutive ones sharing exactly one edge, non-consecutive ones disjoint, the two shared edges of an interior hexagon disjoint), the number of inclusion-maximal matchings of the explicit helicene graph with n hexagons is at most that of G. The equivalence between the source's definition (a plane graph whose bounded faces are hexagons arranged in a chain) and the existence of such a witness, and the identification of the Lean helicene with the source's helicene, are proved in the paper in prose, because Mathlib has no plane embeddings. The minimizer is not unique at n = 4 (the zigzag chain ties at 288); for n = 5 to 10 the helicene and its mirror image are the only minimizers (referee's enumeration of 9,841 chains).

earlier_prior_art_note.sweep_lane: candidates-review-R4-opus-20261119-r1/REVIEW-331692.md (Claude Opus 5.5, PASS; required the graph-with-witness endpoint)

caveats: The kernel-checked endpoint is stated for graphs with a hexagon-chain witness; the passage from the source's plane-graph definition to the witness (and back) is prose, not Lean, since Mathlib has no plane embeddings. An independent referee judged that bridge sound and complete. No uniqueness claim (the helicene ties with the zigzag chain at n = 4). Chen and Zhang (Filomat 2025) still list the problem as open.

rows.title: The unlabelled bridge-addable fragment-size conjecture
rows.record_statement:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a class of graphs that is **bridge-addable**, meaning that adding an edge between vertices in distinct components preserves membership, and **decomposable**, meaning that a graph belongs to $\mathcal A$ if and only if each of its components does. For a graph $G$, define its **fragment size** by

$$
\operatorname{frag}(G)=|V(G)|-\max\{|V(C)|:C\text{ is a component of }G\}.
$$

Let $\tilde{R}_n \in_u\tilde{\mathcal A}$ be sampled uniformly from the unlabelled graphs in $\mathcal A$ on $n$ vertices. **Unlabelled bridge-addable fragment-size conjecture.** For each such graph class $\mathcal A$, there is a constant $c_{\mathcal A}$ such that, for each positive integer $n$,

$$
\mathbb E[\operatorname{frag}(\tilde{R}_n)]\leq c_{\mathcal A}.
$$

The labelled analogue has a uniform expectation bound, while the source gives an unlabelled example showing that the expectation can grow linearly for a particular class; the conjectured bound remains open in general.
rows.source: Colin McDiarmid, “Connectivity for an unlabelled bridge-addable graph class”, arXiv:2001.05256 (2020).
rows.what_was_proved: McDiarmid's Conjecture 3 (the expected fragment size of a uniformly random unlabelled n-vertex graph from a decomposable, bridge-addable class is bounded by a universal constant) is false: there is one fixed isomorphism-invariant, decomposable, bridge-addable class of graphs, with members at every positive order, whose mean fragment size over isomorphism classes of n-vertex members is unbounded in n. The class consists of graphs whose bridgeless pieces are single vertices or members of a staged family of cyclic-layer graphs with very many isomorphism types; the bound obtained is of order t^2/6 at stage t. The first stage begins at about 2^86 vertices, so the effect is invisible at any computable size (below 2^85 vertices the class is exactly the forests).
caveats: The formalized class differs in detail from the one in the discovery proof (the paper proves the formalized one; an independent referee re-derived every inequality). The first stage starts near 2^86 vertices, so no direct numerical confirmation at true size is possible; scaled-down copies were checked. The same class refutes the sibling record MathDB 345191 (Conjecture 4), which is not claimed separately. Bounded literature search; both papers citing the source treat the unlabelled conjectures…

rows.title: Unique permutation with maximal stabilization
rows.record_statement:
Let $w$ be a permutation of $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, viewed as a tableau, and let $\stab(w)$ denote its stabilization time. **Maximal-stabilization conjecture.** The increasing permutation

$$
w=1\,2\,\dots\,(n-1)\,n
$$

is the only permutation with $\stab(w)=n$. This asks for the rightmost entry in the stabilization distribution on permutations to be unique. The statement is posed as an open problem after the paper notes that the leftmost entry is always $1$; its truth is not established there.
rows.source: Connor Ahlbach, “Tableau Stabilization and Rectangular Tableaux Fixed by Promotion Powers”, arXiv:1907.00105 (2020).
rows.what_was_proved: For every n >= 1 and every permutation w of size n, the stabilization index of w equals n if and only if w is the identity: the increasing permutation stabilizes at n, and every permutation with a descent stabilizes by n-1. This proves Ahlbach's conjecture that the increasing permutation is the unique permutation with maximal stabilization. Lean defines stabilization through the row-insertion tableau of the k-fold reading word and checks that every entry of the last copy stays in its original row; the identification of this with the source's definition by jeu de taquin rectification is the source's Lemma 2.10 (a classical theorem of Schutzenberger, cited from Fulton), which is not checked in Lean. The hypothesis n >= 1 is needed and matches the source.
caveats: The kernel-checked definition of stabilization is the row-insertion form; the bridge to the source's rectification form is the classical identity Rect(S) = P(reading word of S) (source Lemma 2.10, from Fulton), trusted and not formalized. An independent referee computed stabilization both ways for all 46,233 permutations with n <= 8 and found agreement, and agreement with Ahlbach's published distribution. Bounded literature search; two citation indexes refused requests.

rows.title: Orientation invariance conjecture for s-permutree lattices
rows.record_statement:
Fix an $n$-tuple ${\boldsymbol{s}}$ of non-negative integers and a decoration map ${\boldsymbol{\delta}}$ assigning one of the four local orientations—none, up, down, or up-down—to each index $i$ with $s_i\ne0$. Let $W_{\boldsymbol{s}}/\equiv_{\boldsymbol{\delta}}$ be the ${\boldsymbol{\delta}}$-permutree lattice, and let its canonical join complex be the simplicial complex formed by canonical join representations.

**Orientation invariance conjecture for s-permutree lattices.** For fixed ${\boldsymbol{s}}$, changing any up decoration to a down decoration in ${\boldsymbol{\delta}}$ does not affect the cardinality of the ${\boldsymbol{\delta}}$-permutree lattice or the $f$-vector of its canonical join complex.

The conjecture concerns invariants that remain unchanged under the indicated decoration change, while the source notes that other structures, such as the undirected cover graph and face lattices, can depend on the positions of the up and down decorations. No resolution is supplied.
rows.source: Eva Philippe and Vincent Pilaud, “Geometric realizations of the s-weak order and its lattice quotients”, arXiv:2405.02092 (2025).
rows.what_was_proved: For every n, every tuple s of non-negative integers (zero entries allowed), every decoration of the other positions and every position k decorated up, changing the decoration at k from up to down changes neither the number of elements of the delta-permutree lattice (the quotient of the s-weak order by the lattice congruence generated by the decoration) nor, for any m, the number of faces of size m of its canonical join complex. This is Conjecture 76 of Philippe and Pilaud. Lean formalizes the objects literally: s-trees and their order with a proved lattice structure, s-arcs, the generated congruence (proved to contract exactly the forbidden arcs), the quotient lattice and canonical join representations defined lattice-theoretically; the proof identifies faces with marked arc diagrams by a sweep bijection and proves the forward direction of the source's Theorem 72 by a direct congruence construction.

earlier_prior_art_note.sweep_lane: shard016-candidate-review-opus-20261119-r1/REVIEW-362959.md (Claude Opus 5.5, PASS, FLAGS none; required the literal lattice-theoretic endpoint)

caveats: Bounded literature search only. A later paper on framing lattices (von Bell and Ceballos, arXiv:2512.20575) covers the s-weak order and classical permutree lattices but not s-permutree lattices or this conjecture; it suggests a possible alternative route that is not published. The case s = (1,...,1) is close to a known classical statement (Pilaud-Pons 2018, cardinality only).

rows.title: Sharpness conjecture for the radio-k-number of even cycles
rows.record_statement:
Let $n$ be even and $k$ be odd with

$$
\frac{n}{2} \leqslant k < n-3.
$$

Set

$$
h=\frac{n-k-1}{2},\qquad p=\gcd(n,h).
$$

Write $\langle h\rangle$ for the subgroup generated by $h$ in the relevant cyclic group. **Sharpness conjecture.** If $n/2\in\langle h\rangle$, then

$$
\operatorname{rn}_k(C_n)=\operatorname{LB}(n,k)+p-1.
$$

The paper notes that the values of the radio $k$-number are known for most parameters in the stated range, but cases with different parities remain open. The conjecture asserts that the upper bound from the preceding theorem is sharp whenever $n/2\in\langle h\rangle$.
rows.source: Colin Bloomfield, Daphne Der-Fen Liu and Jeannette Ramirez, “Radio-k-Labeling of Cycles for Large k”, arXiv:2106.15059 (2022).
rows.what_was_proved: For every even n and odd k with n/2 <= k < n-3, with h = (n-k-1)/2 and p = gcd(n,h), if n/2 lies in the subgroup of Z_n generated by h then the radio-k-number of the cycle C_n equals LB(n,k) + p - 1. This is Conjecture 1 of Bloomfield, Liu and Ramirez. The upper bound is the source's Theorem 11; the new part is the matching lower bound, where the source proves only LB + ceil(p/2) - 1. The proof makes the source's gap lemma quantitative, maps vertices to residues modulo p, and rules out the case where the resulting closed walk wraps around, which is exactly the factor of two the source left open. Lean states the conjecture literally: the graph distance of Mathlib's cycle graph, the radio inequality over the integers, the radio-k-number as a minimum span, and LB proved equal to the source's formula.

rows.title: Fixed-point product formula conjecture for evacuation of Kreweras words
rows.record_statement:
Let $n\geq 1$, and let $\operatorname{{Evac}}$ and $\operatorname{{Evac}}^{*}$ denote the two evacuation operations on Kreweras words of length $3n$. For a word $w$, consider the fixed-point conditions $\operatorname{{Evac}}^{*}(w)=w$ and $\operatorname{{Evac}}(w)=w$.

**Evacuation fixed-point conjecture.** For all $n\geq 1$, the number of Kreweras words of length $3n$ satisfying $\operatorname{{Evac}}^{*}(w)=w$ is

$$
\frac{3^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} 4^{\lceil n/2 \rceil} \prod_{j=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}(3j-1) \prod_{j=1}^{\lceil n/2 \rceil}(3j-2) }{(n+1)!}.
$$

The number satisfying $\operatorname{{Evac}}(w)=w$ is the same when $n$ is even and is $0$ when $n$ is odd. These formulas provide product expressions for the evacuation fixed points, while their status beyond the conjecture is not established in the supplied text.
rows.source: Sam Hopkins and Martin Rubey, “Promotion of Kreweras words”, arXiv:2005.14031 (2021).
rows.what_was_proved: For every n >= 1, the number of Kreweras words of length 3n fixed by dual evacuation equals the product P(n) of Hopkins and Rubey's Conjecture 6.3, and the number fixed by evacuation equals P(n) for even n and 0 for odd n. The proof passes through Stanley's correspondence between evacuation-fixed linear extensions and domino chains of order ideals, then unfolds the reachable states, which fall into three parity sectors, into lattice walks with steps (1,1), (-1,0), (0,-1) that avoid a half-line (the new step), and counts those walks by Bousquet-Melou's slit-plane method: the walk series are T and X*T^2 with T = 1 + 4t^3T^3. Lean formalizes the words, the swap operators, evacuation and dual evacuation literally, with bridge theorems to the source's poset formulation, and proves the walk enumeration for this step set from scratch (61 modules).

rows.title: Strong anti-diagonal eigenvalue property conjecture for stochastic matrices
rows.record_statement: Let $A$ be a stochastic matrix with distinct eigenvalues. Say that $A$ has the **strong anti-diagonal eigenvalue property** when it satisfies the stronger anti-diagonal eigenvalue condition defined in the paper, and let $H^\lambda$ denote the parameterized family of lower-triangular matrices introduced there. **Strong anti-diagonal eigenvalue property conjecture.** $A$ has the strong anti-diagonal eigenvalue property if and only if it is of the form $H^\lambda$. The conjecture would classify stochastic matrices with distinct eigenvalues satisfying this strengthened spectral property; the paper states that it can be proved for $n\leqslant4$, while the general case is left open.
rows.source: John R. Britnell and Mark Wildon, “Involutive random walks on total orders and the anti-diagonal eigenvalue property”, arXiv:2102.08469 (2021).
rows.what_was_proved: For every n and every row-stochastic n x n matrix A with n distinct eigenvalues, A has the global anti-diagonal eigenvalue property (every leading block is lower triangular and real diagonalizable, and the eigenvalues of the block times the reversal matrix are the signed diagonal entries with multiplicity) if and only if A is a binomial transform B Diag(a) B^{-1} of some vector a. This is Conjecture 2.6 of Britnell and Wildon. The source proves the easy direction, the converse away from an exceptional algebraic set, and the cases n <= 4. The proof here is by induction on the size: a maximum principle for iterated finite differences of the eigenvectors forces them into a polynomial flag when the last parameter is positive, and a determinant identity excludes the remaining zero case because it would repeat an eigenvalue. Lean states the property block by block as the conjecture does, not through the eigenbasis property of the source's Theorem 2.9, and assumes no moment representation.

rows.title: Conjectures on successive threshold values for equal-product partitions
rows.record_statement:
For integers $r\geq2$ and $n\geq3$, let $s_r^*(n)$ be the smallest positive integer, if it exists, such that every integer $s\geq s_r^*(n)$ has at least $r$ different $n$-partitions with the same sum and product, without requiring all parts across the partitions to be distinct. **Successive-threshold conjectures.** The following assertions are conjectured:

1. For all integers $n\geq9$, $s_{n-2}^*(n)=s_{n-2}^*(n-1)+1$.
2. For all integers $n\geq7$, $s_{n-1}^*(n)=s_{n-1}^*(n-1)+1$.
3. For all integers $n\geq10$, $s_n^*(n)=s_n^*(n-1)+1$.

These statements are motivated by computational data. The inequalities $s_r^*(n)\leq s_r^*(n-1)+1$ are known from the theorem preceding the conjectures, but equality in the three displayed ranges remains open.
rows.source: Byungchul Cha, Adam Claman, Joshua Harrington, Ziyu Liu, Barbara Maldonado, Alexander Miller, Ann Palma, Tony W. H. Wong and Hongkwon V. Yi, “An Investigation on Partitions with Equal Products”, arXiv:1811.07451 (2018).
rows.what_was_proved: All three parts of Conjecture 5.2 of Cha et al. hold: for every n >= 9, s*_{n-2}(n) = s*_{n-2}(n-1) + 1; for every n >= 7, s*_{n-1}(n) = s*_{n-1}(n-1) + 1; for every n >= 10, s*_n(n) = s*_n(n-1) + 1, where s*_r(n) is the least positive integer beyond which every sum has at least r different partitions into n positive parts with a common product. Both thresholds are shown to exist in every case. The proof has three parts: an elementary stability lemma (below twice the number of parts every partition contains a one, so removing a one is a bijection), explicit infinite families of partitions with equal products that settle all large n, and a certified exhaustive computation for the remaining 77 identities with n <= 34, in which 105 non-existence claims are reduced by padding with ones to 14 enumerations. Lean states partitions as multisets of positive integers and the threshold as the least positive permanent-tail bound, exactly as the source does.

rows.title: Four-point optimal-code conjecture for the Hilbert cube
rows.record_statement:
Let $H$ be the Hilbert cube, with standard basis vectors $e_k$, and set

$$
\alpha:=\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi}{3}.
$$

Choose $N\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ such that

$$
\sum_{k\in N}\frac{1}{k^2}=\alpha-1,
$$

and define

$$
s:=\sum_{k=2}^\infty\frac{1}{k}e_k,\qquad t:=\sum_{k\in N}\frac{1}{k}e_k.
$$

**Hilbert-cube four-point conjecture.** The set

$$
\left\{0,\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\alpha\right)e_1+s,e_1+t,\frac{1}{2}\alpha e_1+s-t\right\}
$$

is an optimal code in the Hilbert cube. Numerical experiments on truncations motivate this prediction; the supplied text later confirms that such choices of $N$ exist but notes that the resulting codes are not unique.
rows.source: Emily J. King, Dustin G. Mixon, Hans Parshall and Chris Wells, “Uniquely optimal codes of low complexity are symmetric”, arXiv:2008.12871 (2025).
rows.what_was_proved: For every set N of indices with the sum of 1/k^2 over N equal to sqrt(2) pi / 3 - 1, the four printed points form an optimal code of size 4 in the Hilbert cube: the set has four points, lies in the cube, and every four-point subset of the cube has two distinct points at distance no larger than the smallest distance of the printed set. This is Conjecture 27 of King, Mixon, Parshall and Wells, who proved the three-point case and left four points open. The proof sorts the four points by first coordinate, pushes the extreme ones to the faces, and splits into two cases at the threshold 1 - alpha/2: either one pair is already close, or a weighted sum of five squared distances with weights 1, 1, 2, 1, 1 is bounded by convexity at the corners of each coordinate box. Lean states the cube inside Mathlib's l^2 space with its own distance and quantifies over every four-element subset.

rows.title: The generic-rank conjecture for bipartite circulant graphs
rows.record_statement:
Let $G(n,l)$ be a bipartite circulant graph of the form considered in the paper, and let the generic completion rank be the rank attained by a generic matrix completion. The dimension-count prediction is

$$
n-
\left\lfloor\sqrt{n^2-nl}\right\rfloor.
$$

**Bipartite circulant generic-rank conjecture.** Every graph $G(n,l)$ has generic completion rank predicted by the dimension count; equivalently,

$$
\operatorname{gcr}(G(n,l))=n-\left\lfloor\sqrt{n^2-nl}\right\rfloor.
$$

The paper proves the dimension-count prediction for a subset of these graphs and conjectures it for all bipartite circulant graphs of this form. The claim is presented as unresolved.
rows.source: Daniel Irving Bernstein, Grigoriy Blekherman and Rainer Sinn, “Typical and Generic Ranks in Matrix Completion”, arXiv:1802.09513 (2019).
rows.what_was_proved: For all n > 0 and 0 <= l <= n, the bipartite circulant graph G(n, l) has generic completion rank n - floor(sqrt(n(n - l))), the value predicted by the dimension count. This is Conjecture 5.6 of Bernstein, Blekherman and Sinn, who proved it for special families and named the step that was missing. The upper bound uses a new construction: Fourier vectors with an evenly spaced (Beatty) set of frequencies, so that each frequency class has at most d elements, and a Vandermonde system on the missing diagonals that forces the tangent map to be injective. The lower bound is the dimension count. Lean states generic completion rank literally, as a statement about a nonempty Zariski-open set of partial matrices in both directions, and proves the passage from a nonzero Jacobian minor to such an open set.
